Can someone explain what makes this so challenging and unusual?

Assembly language is a low level language. What can be written in 2 lines in C++ takes about 9-10 in Assembly. It's the lowest level language that gives orders to the processor itself on how to move data around. It literally deals with 1s and 0s. To have coded such a game with that language is borderline incomprehensible. I can't even wrap my head around the number of lines of code the guy had to keep up with.
So is it a big benefit to code in assembly vs C or something like that? And what would the benefits be?
At best, optimal 100% optimization. But such a thing can still be reached through C at like 95% with premade commands. Mostly he must have done it to cure boredom really.

Benefits are that the computing power requirements of machines to run it can be lower and slower. RCT will run on damn near anything because of its assembly coding. Assembly is a very different language from everything else and is quite hard to read and write. To do what this man has would take monumental mental power and patience. I think 'Sunset Blvd.' is one of the greatest films ever made.

I am about to go watch it. Watching it has been on my to-do list for a while and I think this post is divine intervention telling me to go watch it. I read somewhere that Gloria Swanson's character was based on Norma Talmadge, I am interested to see if that is true. Will report back.

Yup. It lived up to its hype. Some of the shots of the (lack of) door locks were brilliant as was the scene of Gloria Swanson knocking the boom mike away and the scene where William Holden closes the grate doors and talks about prison. The butler coming clean was unexpected. Since you kind of know the ending from the very beginning, the movie has to rely on dialogue and good acting. The scene with the old timers rushing to meet her on set while the young set workers stayed back seemed so authentic. Cecil B. Demille was obviously a better director than an actor, but that has to be a challenge to play yourself in a movie. The whole movie seemed very meta. Gloria Swanson's character could have been based on any number of former actresses from the silent era, or even the early sound era. The only connections to from the character Norma to the real Norma Talmadge that I saw were that both owned a lot of real estate and a big house and both were cast aside during the transition to sound (and of course the first name).

I've also heard that Swanson's character was based on Norma Talmadge, which makes sense because her popularity also dwindled with audiences when talkies marked the end for silent films. I hope you enjoyed it :)
